lessons.title: Who is that boy? (Describing people)
match: Talking about one's family members, friends…
objectives: Describe and identify people: appearance, clothes and personality.
Use What does he look like? / What is he like? and who / whose.
lessons.intro: I show a photo of a person and ask: “Who is this? What does he look like? What is he wearing? What is he like?”
lessons.summary: The teacher shows a picture of Harouna, a former student. The students describe him: he is wearing a green T-shirt, he is handsome with black curly hair and brown skin, and he is polite, confident and smart. In the second dialogue, the school chooses the student of the year: Mohamed, who is hardworking, cooperative, polite, sociable, humble and reliable. To ask about appearance: What does he look like? – He is tall / He has curly hair. To ask about personality: What is he like? – He is humble. To identify: the boy with the green T-shirt, the man in the white boubou, the girl whose shirt is yellow.
points: Appearance: What does he look like? – He is tall / He has curly hair.
Personality: What is he like? – He is humble and hard-working.
Clothes: He is wearing a green T-shirt.
Identify: the man in the white boubou / the man with the big nose.
Relative pronouns: who, whose, that, which.

lessons.title: Past actions and events
match: Talking about one's, a friend's, a neighbor's… experience and past actions
objectives: Talk about past actions and events.
Use the simple past (affirmative, negative, interrogative).
lessons.intro: I ask: “What did you do last weekend? Where did you go?”
lessons.summary: The text compares science in the past and today. In the past, scientists worked with very simple tools and observed the sky with their naked eyes; in 1609 Galileo observed the stars with his first telescope; researchers measured everything by hand and wrote their results in notebooks; in 1928 Fleming searched for a way to fight bacteria. Today science moves much faster. We use the simple past for finished past actions: regular verbs + -ed (worked, observed), irregular verbs (spent, took). Negative: didn’t + base verb. Question: Did + subject + base verb?
points: Simple past: finished actions in the past.
Regular verbs: work → worked, observe → observed.
Irregular verbs: spend → spent, take → took.
Negative: didn’t + base verb.
Question: Did + subject + base verb?

application.q: Put into the past: Scientists (work) with simple tools. They (not / have) computers.
application.a: Scientists worked with simple tools. They didn’t have computers.

lines: Affirmative: Scientists worked with simple tools.
Negative: They didn’t have computers.
Question: Did they share ideas by letters?
Regular: work → worked – observe → observed
Irregular: spend → spent – take → took
Put into the past: Scientists (work) with simple tools. They (not / have) computers.

lessons.title: Expressing simultaneity (while, when, as)
objectives: Talk about actions happening at the same time in the past.
Use while, when and as with the past continuous.
lessons.intro: I ask: “What were you doing yesterday at 8 p.m.? What was your brother doing at the same time?”
lessons.summary: The student tells the teacher about his busy afternoon: while he was working on his homework, his little brother was watching TV; when his father came home, his brother was still watching TV. We use while for two long actions at the same time: while + past continuous, past continuous. We use when for a short action that happens during a longer one: when + simple past, past continuous. We use as for two background actions happening together.
points: While + past continuous + past continuous.
When + simple past + past continuous.
As + past continuous + past continuous.
Past continuous: was/were + verb-ing.

application.q: Rewrite with when: I was sleeping. The phone rang.
application.a: When the phone rang, I was sleeping.

lines: Two long actions: While I was studying, my brother was watching TV.
Short action during a long one: When the bell rang, we were writing.
Background actions: As I was walking, I was thinking.
Rewrite with when: I was sleeping. The phone rang.

lessons.title: Talking about the future
match: Talking about one's, a friend's, a neighbor's… future life and intentions
objectives: Talk about future actions and plans.
lessons.intro: I ask: “What will you do after the exams? What will you be in the future?”
lessons.summary: Ahmed and Mariem talk about the government’s future transport projects: SNIM will modernize the railway between Zouerate and Nouadhibou, the government will build new roads, and the ports of Nouakchott and Nouadhibou will be expanded. We use will / shall + base verb for the future. Negative: will not (won’t) / shall not (shan’t). Question: Will / Shall + subject + base verb? Shall is mainly used with I and we, for offers and suggestions.
points: Will / shall + base verb.
Negative: won’t / shan’t + base verb.
Question: Will you help me tomorrow?
Shall with I / we: Shall we start the lesson now?

application.q: Make negative and interrogative: She will start a new job next week.
application.a: She won’t start a new job next week. Will she start a new job next week?

lines: Affirmative: The government will build new roads.
Negative: They won’t arrive today.
Question: Will you help me tomorrow?
Will: all subjects – decisions, promises, predictions
Shall: I / we – offers and suggestions
Make negative and interrogative: She will start a new job next week.

lessons.title: Real conditions (promises)
match: Making promises and expressing the likelihood of happenings
objectives: Make promises and express likely results.
Use the zero and first conditionals.
lessons.intro: I ask: “What will your parents do if you pass your exam?”
lessons.summary: A son asks his father: “What will you do for me if I pass my final exam?” The father promises: “If you pass, I’ll take you on a nice trip.” Zero conditional (facts, routines): If + present simple, present simple – If you heat water, it boils. First conditional (real future possibilities): If + present simple, will + base verb – If you study hard, you will succeed.
points: Zero conditional: If + present, present (facts).
First conditional: If + present, will + base verb.
Promises: If you pass, I’ll take you on a trip.
Likely results: If it rains, we will stay home.

application.a: If you speak English every day, you will improve quickly.

lines: If + present simple, present simple

lessons.title: Making comparison (superlatives)
match: Comparing people and things using the superlatives
objectives: Compare people and things using comparatives and superlatives.
Use the superlative of superiority and inferiority.
lessons.intro: I ask: “What is the biggest city in Mauritania? Who is the tallest student in our class?”
lessons.summary: The text compares students and places in a school: Mariem is more intelligent than Ahmed, Hamoud is faster. We use the superlative to show that one thing is the most or the least in a group. Superiority: short adjectives: the + adjective + -est (the tallest); long adjectives: the most + adjective (the most intelligent). Inferiority: the least + adjective (the least careful). Example: Nouakchott is the biggest city in Mauritania.
points: Comparative: taller than, more beautiful than.
Superlative (short): the + adj + -est – the tallest.
Superlative (long): the most + adj – the most intelligent.
Inferiority: the least + adj – the least interesting.

application.q: Complete: Nouakchott is ____ (big) city in Mauritania. Fatima is ____ (hardworking) student.

lines: Short: the + adj + -est – Ali is the tallest student.
Long: the most + adj – Mariem is the most intelligent girl.
the least + adj – This is the least interesting book.
Nouakchott is the biggest city in Mauritania.
Complete: Nouakchott is ____ (big) city in Mauritania. Fatima is ____ (hardworking) student.
